headline: Want to testify to Congress? Ask the White House first.
summary: White House counsel Will Scharf told every federal agency on Monday to get his office's approval before any employee agrees to testify to Congress. Democrats take both chambers in January and have promised investigations. A White House official said the administration "will not be extorted" by "baseless" probes.

cover_question.q: Who gets to say no to Congress?

cover_answer: The White House lawyer, it says. He screens every request.
table_question: Should the person being checked get to decide what counts as fair?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The people who work for the president got a new rule today. Before they go and answer questions from Congress, the big group of lawmakers, they have to ask the president's lawyer first. It's like raising your hand before you leave the table. Nobody is in trouble, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: At six the raised hand is the rule. The fight over it can wait.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reads your face before your words, so the script keeps this as a rule about asking first, the raised hand at the table, with nothing to fear in it. At this age the concrete thing is a permission slip, so that is what they get. Expect "did someone do something bad?" No. They changed who says yes.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: In January Democrats take over Congress, promising to investigate the president's team. Congress does that by calling workers in to answer questions. Monday's memo says no worker may go until the White House lawyer signs off. A gate on an open path, and he decides what's "reasonable".
8-12.why: At eight, who holds the gate is a fairness question, and they ask it unprompted.
8-12.why_long: At eight a child is working out rules and whether the grown-ups apply them fairly, and this story is a rule about rules. The gate gives it a shape: an open path, a new gatekeeper, and the gatekeeper deciding what is reasonable. Expect "is that allowed?" The White House says yes. Congress has not answered yet.

13-17.script: Who decides if an investigation is legitimate: the people doing it, or the people under it? The White House lawyer will now clear every official before they testify, and calls the coming probes "baseless". Second: he cited the Supreme Court: Congress can't investigate to punish. Where's the line?
13-17.why: A real line exists. So does an interest in drawing it. They can hold both.
13-17.why_long: At sixteen they can argue where a line sits, and this story is the line: the Supreme Court says Congress can't investigate to punish, and the people drawing it are the ones who would be investigated. Kuhn says arguing is practised. Expect "so who checks the checker?" You don't know yet. That is the fight.

5-7.a: A big group of people the country voted for. They make the laws.

8-12.q: Who gets to say no to Congress?
8-12.a: The White House lawyer, it says. He passes the reasonable ones.

8-12.q: Why do Democrats want to investigate?
8-12.a: They won big in November and promised to check the administration.

13-17.a: The White House says it's screening. Rep. Garcia says voters want checks.
He doesn't think the Senate has the 67 votes to remove him, Axios says.
